posts.title_en: Thor answered the cross – and fell silent
posts.summary_en: Only seven of 2,321 Swedish runestones bear Thor's name, his hammer or a pagan curse. They were carved while the cross was spreading, among Christian stones, and several imitate the form of the cross. In the Danish realm such stones are five times as common, but they follow the same pattern: they belong to the generations around the conversion and fall silent when the prayer reaches the stones. We think Thor came to the runestones as an answer to the new faith.
posts.body_en:
*Þyrvé raised the stone in memory of Ôgmundr, her husband, a very good thegn. May Thor hallow.*

So it reads on a runestone at Velanda in Västergötland. The last two words, *Þórr vígi*, ask Thor to hallow the stone. It is one of the clearest pagan invocations on any Swedish runestone – and it has almost no company. Of 2,321 Swedish runestones only seven bear Thor's name, his hammer, a picture from the myths about him or a pagan curse. A cross or a Christian prayer is found on 1,103. Why are the old powers so rare? We followed the seven stones through time, through the landscape and among the stones that have been lost – and then ran the same test in the Danish realm.

![The runestone Vg 150](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/57/Velandastenen.jpg)
Vg 150 at Velanda in Västergötland. The text ends with *Þórr vígi*, may Thor hallow. Photo: Tubaist (sv.wikipedia), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Velandastenen.jpg).

:::box In short
- Only seven Swedish runestones have pagan words or images. Six are about Thor, the seventh bears a curse. Several imitate the Christian stone: the hammer stands where the cross usually stands, and *may Thor hallow* stands where the prayer usually stands.
- They were carved while the cross was spreading, mainly in the first half of the eleventh century, and they stand among Christian stones as densely as other stones of the same time – not in remote, pagan districts.
- In the Danish realm pagan markers are about five times as common, even when we compare stones of the same time. But they follow the same pattern: they belong to the generations around the conversion and fall silent when the prayer reaches the stones. In Denmark it begins and ends earlier – as did the conversion.
- The lost stones do not change the picture, and the traces of iconoclasm are weak: half of the stones built into churches bore a cross or a prayer themselves.
- Our hypothesis: Thor and the old powers were given words on the runestones during the generations when the new faith pressed in, and fell silent once it had won. It can be tested.
:::

## What binds the seven together?

We went through the 2,321 Swedish runestones in the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base and looked for pagan and ritual markers: Thor's name in the text, formulas such as *Þórr vígi* (may Thor hallow) and *vígi þessi kuml* (hallow this monument), curses, the old magical word *alu*, and images of Thor's hammer or of Thor fishing for the Midgard serpent.

:::box The seven stones
- **Ög 136, Rök.** Thor's name appears in Rundata's interpretation of the long, enigmatic text. The stone is older than the others, probably from the ninth century.
- **Sö 111, Stenkvista.** A Thor's hammer, carved where the cross usually sits.
- **Sö 140, Korpbron.** *May Thor protect*, an uncertain reading. The text ends with a cross-shaped bind-rune.
- **Sö 352, Linga.** Thor's fishing on the front – and a cross on the back.
- **Vg 67, Saleby.** A curse on whoever destroys the stone: he shall become *ræti* and *argR kona*, in Rundata's translation a warlock and a maleficent woman.
- **Vg 150, Velanda.** *Þórr vígi*, may Thor hallow, at the end of the text.
- **U 1161, Altuna.** Thor's fishing, on a stone carved by Balli, Frøysteinn and Lífsteinn.
:::

The first thing that binds them together is the god. Six of the seven are about Thor; none names Odin, Freyr or any other god. Thor was the thunder god and the protector, the one who fought the Midgard serpent. In the Icelandic stories of the conversion, too, it is Thor who challenges Christ. The seventh, Saleby, names no god but threatens whoever harms the monument with shame and sorcery.

The second is that they borrow from the Christian stone. The hammer at Stenkvista stands where the cross usually stands. The text at Korpbron ends with a bind-rune in the shape of a cross. The stone at Linga has Thor on one side and a cross on the other. And *may Thor hallow* stands at the end of the text, where the Christian stones have their prayer. The Altuna stone was carved by Balli with two others, and Balli also made Christian stones: 29 of his 76 stones have a cross. Otherwise they are ordinary runestones: they were raised in memory of fathers, a son, a husband, a wife, a brother and kinsmen – by sons, a father, a widow, a husband and a sister.

One more stone belongs to the same picture. At Åby in Södermanland there is a Thor's hammer and perhaps a Thor's mask on an earth-fast boulder (Sö 86). It is not counted among the runestones here, since it is carved on a boulder lying where it has always lain.

![The runestone Sö 111](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/S%C3%B6_111%2C_Stenkvista.jpg/960px-S%C3%B6_111%2C_Stenkvista.jpg)
Sö 111 at Stenkvista church in Södermanland. Where the cross usually sits, the carver made a Thor's hammer. Photo: Berig, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:S%C3%B6_111,_Stenkvista.jpg).

## When were they carved?

Six of the stones can be dated by their ornament. Five belong to the two earliest style groups, RAK and Fp, the time up to about 1050. The sixth, the Altuna stone, belongs to Pr3, about 1050–1080. No pagan stone is younger than that. It was just in that time that the cross was spreading: Christian markers are found on 55 % of the stones in RAK and on 75 % in Fp.

:::chart Share of runestones with Christian markers, by style group
+RAK, around 1000 | 55 | 169 stones, 2 with pagan markers
+Fp, around 1030 | 75 | 149 stones, 3 with pagan markers
Pr1, around 1030 | 80 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 82 | 87 stones
+Pr3, around 1065 | 69 | 118 stones, 1 with pagan markers
Pr4, around 1085 | 68 | 198 stones
Pr5, around 1115 | 66 | 32 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis of the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base; stones with a legible text, dated by their style group (Gräslund 2006). Christian markers: a cross or a Christian prayer or formula.
:::

Seven stones are not enough for firm statistics, and we want to be honest about it. The two earliest style groups hold 40 % of all dated stones. Five out of six in them would therefore happen by chance in about 4 cases in 100. That no pagan stone is younger than Pr3, although 30 % of the dated stones are, would happen by chance in about 12 cases in 100. The pattern points to the breakthrough of the conversion, but it cannot carry a conclusion on its own.

## A land in the middle of a change of faith

In the first half of the eleventh century Sweden was on its way to becoming Christian, but was not yet. Olof Skötkonung, the first Swedish king we know was baptised, had coins struck at Sigtuna around the year 1000, some with crosses after English models. Västergötland got a bishop at Skara in the first half of the eleventh century. But around 1075 Adam of Bremen describes a great pagan temple at Uppsala, with images of Thor, Odin and Freyr. Thor, he writes, sat in the middle as the mightiest. According to later stories, King Ingi the Elder was driven out for a time because he refused to sacrifice. The conversion went family by family and district by district, over several generations, and the old gods lived on for a long time beside the new one. In that world a runestone was a public statement of where the family stood.

## Where do they stand?

![Pagan or ritual markers on Vitki's pattern map](/figurer/db98b856eca84bd7.webp)
Pagan or ritual markers on Vitki's pattern map. Source: Vitki's pattern map (r/blogfig.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

The seven stones are spread over five provinces, with Södermanland as the centre of gravity: three of seven, although Södermanland has 17 % of the runestones with a legible text. That would happen by chance in about 10 cases in 100 – a hint, not a firm pattern. Two stand in Västergötland, closest to the Danish realm. None stands in eastern Uppland, where the runestones are densest.

The most important question is which stones stood around them. If the pagan stones were remnants of districts that Christianity had not yet reached, their neighbours should have been pagan or silent. That was not so. Among the neighbouring stones within 25 kilometres, from the time up to about 1080, 70 % bear a cross or a Christian prayer – as many as around other stones from the same time (70 %). (Velanda has too few neighbours to be counted.) So the pagan stones did not stand in districts the cross had not yet reached. They stood among the Christian ones.

The old still shows in the landscape, though not in the words. 67 % of the runestones stand within 500 metres of a grave field, mostly from the Iron Age, against 22 % of random places in the same districts. That holds for the Christian stones too: they stand by the grave fields at least as often as the others. Only the bridge stones, raised where the road needed a bridge, stand clearly less often there. Christianity changed the stone's words but not its place.

![The runestones and the ancient monuments: the share within 500 m, against random places in the same districts](/figurer/774192d17776432f.webp)
The runestones and the ancient monuments: the share within 500 m, against random places in the same districts. Source: Vitki's corpus analysis in R (remains.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL); Swedish National Heritage Board.

:::chart Who stands by the grave fields
# Before about 1050 (RAK–Pr2)
+With Christian markers | 70 | 216 stones
Without Christian markers | 55 | 118 stones
# After about 1050 (Pr3–Pr5)
+With Christian markers | 74 | 156 stones
Without Christian markers | 65 | 86 stones
# The bridge stones
+Mention a bridge | 56 | 81 stones
Other stones | 67 | 1016 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis; stones still standing in their place, and the grave fields in the Swedish National Heritage Board's register. Share within 500 m of a grave field; random places in the same districts: 22 %.
:::

## Did the pagan stones disappear?

Perhaps there were more, which have been lost? Rundata knows 415 Swedish runestones that have disappeared since they were described. Many were drawn by the antiquarians of the seventeenth century before they were blasted, built into walls or broken up. For 182 of them the text is known.

None of them has a pagan marker. Had the lost stones been pagan as often as the surviving ones – seven of 1,111 – we would have expected a single one. So the zero says little on its own, but it sets a limit: the share of pagan stones among the lost ones is probably below 2 %. And the lost stones were as Christian as the surviving ones: 66 against 69 % bear a cross or a prayer. With style group and province held constant the odds ratio is 1.1, probably between 0.6 and 2.0 – in practice no difference (p 0.71). The stones lost since the seventeenth century were not different. If pagan stones were destroyed, it happened earlier, and that we cannot see.

## Traces of iconoclasm?

Iconoclasm – deliberately destroying the images and signs of another faith – is a reasonable thought. In the Middle Ages Christian builders built runestones into the walls and foundations of churches. If they chose the pagan or non-Christian stones on purpose, the stones built in should more often lack a cross and a prayer.

Rundata's notes mention 26 dated stones that have been built into churches. Half of them bear a cross or a prayer themselves (50 %), against 62 % of the other stones. Among the stones whose text is so well preserved that a cross and a prayer could have been seen, the difference is 56 against 71 %. That points weakly towards iconoclasm, but a difference this large would arise by chance in about 16 cases in 100 (odds ratio 0.46, probably between 0.16 and 1.34). And the most important point speaks against it: half of the stones built in were Christian themselves. The builders took stone where stone was to be had.

Nor have the pagan images that survive been cut away. Thor's hammer at Stenkvista and Thor's fishing at Altuna can still be seen today.

![The runestone U 1161](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/U1161_Altunastenen_Tors_fiskaf%C3%A4nge_2.jpg/960px-U1161_Altunastenen_Tors_fiskaf%C3%A4nge_2.jpg)
U 1161 at Altuna church in Uppland: Thor in the boat, with the Midgard serpent on the hook. Photo: Gunnar Creutz, [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U1161_Altunastenen_Tors_fiskaf%C3%A4nge_2.jpg).

A tenable hypothesis of iconoclasm must therefore be narrower: that the images of the old gods in particular were sometimes removed, or turned inwards when the stone was built into a wall. It can be tested, but not with Rundata's records.

:::box How sure we are
With so few stones it is easy to see patterns that are not there. So we have been careful:

- **Exact probabilities.** For the seven Swedish and the eight Danish stones we compute exactly how often an equally clear pattern would arise by chance, rather than relying on approximations that need many stones.
- **The same time.** The neighbourhood is compared only with stones from the same time, up to about 1080, and with 20,000 random draws of as many stones. Sweden and Denmark are compared within three periods, so that the difference does not merely reflect that the Danish stones are older.
- **The same search.** The Swedish and the Danish stones were searched with exactly the same markers.
- **The same style group and province.** The lost and the built-in stones are compared with stones from the same style group and province, so that the differences do not merely reflect time or district.
- **A preserved text.** The fair comparison of the built-in stones uses only stones whose text is so well preserved that a cross or a prayer could have been seen.
- **Random places.** The grave fields are compared with random places in the same districts, and only with stones still standing in their original place.
:::

## Why so few? Our hypothesis

That pagan signs are rare on the runestones is known, as are the Danish stones that ask Thor to hallow the runes or the monument. It has also been suggested that the Thor's hammer pendants were an answer to the cross (Nordeide 2006). What we add is the measurement: when the pagan stones were carved compared with the Christian ones, which stones stood around them, that neither the lost nor the built-in stones suggest there were more – and the same test in the neighbouring realm.

Our hypothesis is that Thor came to the runestones as an answer to the cross. Thor was of course there long before the cross. In the Mälaren region some 450 iron rings with small Thor's hammers have been found in graves from the eighth to the tenth century, 58 of them at Birka, almost all in cremation graves (Nordeide 2006, after Wamers). But they lay in the graves, with the dead. On the public stone, which everyone could see, the old faith in Sweden had no tradition of writing its gods. On the earliest stones, in RAK, 44 % lack any religious marker, and only two have pagan words. It was the cross and the prayer that made the runestone a place of faith. When some answered all the same, they did so with the cross's own means – a symbol where the cross used to stand, a prayer at the end of the text – and only during the generation when the question was open. That is why they are so few.

## Denmark: the same pattern, earlier

If Thor was an answer to the new faith, the pagan stones should turn up where and when Christianity came – and in a realm converted earlier they should come earlier. The Danish realm offers a second test. Christianity came there before Sweden. Christian missionaries were at work there in the ninth century, and around 850 the trading town of Hedeby got a church (Rimbert). On the Jelling stone, raised about 965, Harald Bluetooth says that he "made the Danes Christian".

By the Danish realm we mean the realm around the year 1000: today's Denmark with Scania, Blekinge, Bornholm and Schleswig. Rundata has 239 Viking-age runestones from there, and we searched them with exactly the same markers as the Swedish ones. Eight have pagan words or images.

:::box The eight Danish stones
- **DR 209, Glavendrup on Funen.** Ragnhildr raised the stone in memory of Alli, *goði* – priest of the sanctuary. The carver Sóti ends: *may Thor hallow these runes*, and a curse on whoever damages the stone.
- **DR 230, Tryggevælde on Zealand.** Ragnhildr raised the stone in memory of Gunnulfr, her husband, and made a mound and a ship-setting. A curse on whoever damages the stone or drags it away.
- **DR 110, Virring in Jutland.** *May Thor hallow this monument.*
- **DR 81, Skern in Jutland.** Sasgerðr raised the stone in memory of Óðinkárr. *A sorcerer be the man who breaks this monument.*
- **DR 83, Sønder Vinge in Jutland.** Guði and Auði each raised a text in memory of their two brothers, and both curse whoever destroys the memorial.
- **DR 120, Spentrup in Jutland.** Áskatla raised the stone. After the last word divider stands a Thor's hammer.
- **DR 220, Sønder Kirkeby on Falster.** Sassur raised the stone in memory of Ásgautr, his brother, who died on Gotland. *May Thor hallow the runes.*
- **DR 338, Glemminge in Scania.** Sveini raised the stone in memory of Tosti, his father. *May whosoever breaks it become a warlock.*
:::

The first thing that strikes one is how many they are. 3 % of the runestones of the Danish realm have pagan markers, against 0.3 % of the Swedish ones. The Danish stones are older on average, so we also compared stones of the same time: before 1000, 1000–1050 and after 1050. Then pagan markers are about 5 times as common in the Danish realm. A difference like that would arise by chance in about 4 cases in 1,000.

The second is that they speak differently. In Sweden it is Thor's image that stands where the cross usually stands. In Denmark half are curses protecting the monument, and Thor comes as a formula: *may Thor hallow*. We have written about the curses and their path through a thousand years in [Whoever breaks this stone](/artiklar/den-som-bryter-denna-sten). Two of the seven Swedish stones speak Danish formulas – Velanda's *may Thor hallow* and Saleby's curse – and both stand in Västergötland, the province that in other respects too [wrote like the Danes](/artiklar/vastgotarna-skrev-som-danskarna).

The third is time. Rundata dates the Danish stones by rune forms, language and context in periods around the Jelling monuments.

:::chart The Danish realm: share of runestones with a Christian text, by Rundata's period
Helnæs-Gørlev, about 800–900 | 0 | 15 stones
+pre-Jelling, about 900–950 | 0 | 10 stones, 2 with pagan markers
+Jelling, about 950–1000 | 3 | 35 stones, 1 with pagan markers
+post-Jelling, about 1000–1050 | 6 | 108 stones, 5 with pagan markers
1050–1150 | 41 | 44 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis of the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base, the runestones of the Danish realm (DR, with Scania, Blekinge, Bornholm and Schleswig). Christian text: God, Christ, the soul or a prayer in Rundata's translation. Rundata's period Christian post-Jelling is included in post-Jelling.
:::

All eight pagan stones belong to the periods before about 1050. Two are older than Harald's baptism, six are from his time or after. Christian text is rare on all of them: before the year 1000 it is found only on Harald's own Jelling stone, and even in the first half of the eleventh century on only 6 % of the stones. After 1050, 41 % bear a Christian text – and not a single stone has a pagan marker. That would happen by chance in about 15 cases in 100. So the pattern is as weak as the Swedish one if each realm is seen on its own, but it has the same shape: the pagan words belong to the generations when the new faith pressed in, and they fall silent once the prayer has reached the stones. In Denmark it begins around 900 and ends before 1050. In Sweden it belongs to the eleventh century and ends around 1080. The difference follows that of the conversion.

Denmark also changes the picture on one point. There the pagan stones do not stand among Christian stones, for Christian stones hardly existed yet. The cross was in the realm – at the king's Jelling and in the trading towns – but not on the stones of the countryside. There the answer was aimed at the new faith in the realm, not at the neighbour's cross. And the two oldest stones, Ragnhildr's at Glavendrup and Tryggevælde, show that the old powers could be given words on stone before the king's baptism. Whether the Ragnhildr of the two stones is the same woman has long been debated. Her husband Alli at Glavendrup was a *goði*, a priest of the old sanctuary.

So we state the hypothesis like this:

> Thor and the old powers were given words on the runestones during the generations when the new faith pressed into the realm, and fell silent once it had won. They were an answer, not a survival.

The test has its limits: the stones are seven in Sweden and eight in Denmark, the datings are rough, and each realm on its own gives only a hint.

## How the hypothesis can be tested further

1. **The pendants.** Research distinguishes an older tradition with several small hammers on an iron ring from a younger one with a single hammer as a pendant, and it is the pendant that can be compared with the cross pendant (Staecker and Gräslund, according to Nordeide 2006). The pendants and their moulds have been found mainly in southern Sweden, Denmark and northern Germany, and only about one in ten in a grave. If the hammer was an answer to the cross, the single pendants should be most common where and when the crosses came. That can be tested once the pendants are compiled with find-place and date. One such object is in Rundata: a copper amulet from Södra Kvinneby on Öland (Öl SAS1989;43), which asks Thor to protect Bófi with his hammer.
2. **Norway.** A third realm, converted by its kings around the year 1000, can show whether the old powers are always given words in the generations of the conversion.
3. **The families.** If the pagan stones were an answer in a local struggle, the families behind them may have been neighbours or kin of those who raised Christian stones. The names on the stones can be tested in Vitki's network analysis.
4. **The built-in stones.** A survey of how the stones sat in the church walls – which side was turned outwards – can test the narrower hypothesis of iconoclasm.

## Caveats

- Seven Swedish and eight Danish stones are not enough for statistics. The probabilities above are exact, but they rest on very few cases.
- Our search rests on Rundata's text, translation and notes and can miss images not described there. A stone without Christian markers is not thereby pagan.
- The Danish stones are dated differently from the Swedish ones, and the dating rests partly on the content. Rundata's period "Christian post-Jelling" presupposes a Christian text, so we have merged it with post-Jelling and test only whether any pagan stone is younger than 1050.
- Rundata records crosses on far fewer Danish stones than Swedish ones. For Denmark we therefore count only Christian text, not crosses.
- The Rök stone is counted here in the earliest style group but is probably older, from the ninth century.
- The lost stones are only those described before they disappeared. Stones destroyed in the Middle Ages, before anyone wrote them down, do not show at all.
- The records of built-in stones come from Rundata's free notes and are not complete.
- The grave fields in the register are mostly undated, and the register is unevenly complete in different districts.
- An association is not a cause. The hypothesis explains the pattern, but other explanations are possible – for example that the pagan simply did not belong on a memorial stone, before and after the conversion.

:::box The essentials in brief
- Of 2,321 Swedish runestones, only seven bear Thor, his hammer or a pagan curse – against more than a thousand with a cross or a prayer.
- The seven are not remnants of an older, pagan age in remote districts: they were carved while the cross was spreading, amid Christian stones, and several mimic the cross's place and the prayer's place in the text.
- In the Danish realm the stones spoke with the old powers more often, but the pattern is the same: the pagan words belong to the generations around the conversion and fall silent when the prayer reaches the stones. Christianity came earlier there, and so Thor came and went earlier too.
- Our hypothesis to test: Thor lived long in the graves, but on the public stone he was given words only when the new faith called for an answer.
:::

## See for yourself

![Christian markers on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050](/figurer/86e8f5f7b4cd3501.webp)
Christian markers on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050. Source: Vitki's pattern map (r/blogfig.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

On how the prayer left the stones: [The prayer fell silent – but the cross remained](/artiklar/2026-10-bonen-tystnade-korset-stod-kvar).

The maps, curves and models come from Vitki, an open tool for runestone research that you can download and run on your own computer from [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes). The method is described in [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md).

posts.title: Ristaren tog sista ordet
posts.summary: Omkring 1035 slutade mer än var fjärde runsten med en bön till Gud. Femtio år senare slutade fler med ristarens eget namn. Men signaturen trängde inte undan bönen, och den följde inte efterfrågan – den följde ristarna. Vi tror att den spreds som en sed från mästare till lärjunge.
posts.body:
*Vidhugse lät resa denna sten efter sin gode fader. Han bodde i Ågersta. Här ska stenen stå mellan gårdarna. Må den som är kunnig i runor tyda de runor som Balle ristade.*

Så står det på en runsten vid Ågersta i Uppland, ristad någon gång mellan 1050 och 1080 att döma av ornamentiken. Faderns namn kan tolkas på två sätt, men om ristaren råder ingen tvekan: Balle sätter sitt namn sist, efter en uppmaning till den som kan läsa. Han var inte ensam. På de tidigaste runstenarna nämns ristaren nästan aldrig, men på de sista står ristarens namn på mer än var tredje sten, och nästan alltid allra sist. Det sista ordet, som en generation tidigare ofta var en bön till Gud, blev ristarens.

![Runstenen U 729](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg/960px-U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg)
U 729 vid Ågersta i Uppland, ristad av Balle. Texten slutar med *de runor som Balle ristade*. Foto: Bengt A. Lundberg, [CC BY 2.5 SE](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5/se/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg).

:::box Kort sagt
- Ristarens namn – signaturen – står på 3 % av de tidigaste runstenarna och på 38 % av de sista, nästan alltid sist i texten.
- Omkring 1035 slutade fler texter med en bön än med ristarens namn. Femtio år senare var det tvärtom: det sista ordet hade gått från Gud till ristaren.
- Men signaturen trängde inte undan bönen på stenarna, och den var inte vanligare där det restes många stenar. Den följde ristarna: somliga signerade var tredje sten, andra nästan aldrig.
- Vår hypotes: signaturen spreds som en sed mellan ristarna, från mästare till lärjunge, inte som svar på beställarnas efterfrågan. Den kan prövas.
:::

## Sista ordet byter ägare

Vi gick igenom de 1 292 runstenar i Sverige som har en läsbar text i Samnordisk runtextdatabas. På 182 av dem har ristaren skrivit sitt namn, med en ristarformel som *Balli risti*, Balle ristade. Nio av tio signaturer står bland textens fem sista ord. Bönen – *Gud hjälpe hans själ* – står också oftast sist. Och på de 36 stenar som har både en bön och en signatur kommer signaturen efter bönen, på varenda en. Ristaren tar sista ordet, efter Gud.

Därför kan man följa hur texterna slutar. 740 av de daterade stenarna har ett bevarat slut.

:::chart Hur texten slutar, efter stilgrupp
# Med en bön
RAK, omkring 1000 | 10 | 155 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 23 | 137 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 19 | 47 stenar
+Pr2, omkring 1035 | 27 | 81 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 22 | 111 stenar
Pr4, omkring 1085 | 7 | 180 stenar
Pr5, omkring 1115 | 3 | 29 stenar
# Med ristarens namn
RAK, omkring 1000 | 2 | 155 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 7 | 137 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 13 | 47 stenar
Pr2, omkring 1035 | 12 | 81 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 22 | 111 stenar
+Pr4, omkring 1085 | 22 | 180 stenar
+Pr5, omkring 1115 | 38 | 29 stenar
Källa: Vitkis korpusanalys av Samnordisk runtextdatabas; stenar med bevarat slut, daterade efter sin stilgrupp (Gräslund 2006).
:::

Omkring 1035, i stilgruppen Pr2, slutar 27 % av texterna med en bön och 12 % med ristarens namn. En generation senare, i Pr3, är de lika vanliga, 22 % vardera. I Pr4, omkring 1085, har förhållandet vänt: 7 % slutar med en bön och 22 % med ristarens namn. Bland de sista runstenarna, i Pr5, slutar 38 % med ristarens namn och 3 % med en bön.

## Signaturen breder ut sig

Räknar vi alla daterade stenar, inte bara dem med bevarat slut, står ristarens namn på 3 % av de tidigaste (RAK) och på 38 % av de sista (Pr5).

:::chart Andel runstenar med ristarens namn, efter stilgrupp
+RAK, omkring 1000 | 3 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 7 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 16 | 51 stenar
Pr2, omkring 1035 | 13 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 23 | 118 stenar
Pr4, omkring 1085 | 23 | 198 stenar
+Pr5, omkring 1115 | 38 | 32 stenar
Källa: som ovan, alla daterade stenar med läsbar text.
:::

Vår modell jämför stenar av samma ristare och i samma trakt. Med den stiger andelen från omkring 6 procent omkring år 1000 till 28 procent i början av 1100-talet – en ökning med 22 procentenheter, sannolikt någonstans mellan 10 och 36.

Den sista stapeln kräver en förklaring. 28 av de 32 stenarna i Pr5 är ristade av en och samma ristare, Öpir, som signerade ungefär var tredje sten han gjorde. Den stapeln är alltså till stor del hans. Men ökningen beror inte på honom: utan Öpirs stenar stiger andelen från 3 % i RAK till 23 % i Pr3 och 19 % i Pr4.

![Runstenen U 104](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/U_104%2C_Ed.jpg/960px-U_104%2C_Ed.jpg)
U 104 vid Eds kyrka i Uppland, en av Öpirs stenar. Texten slutar *ØpiR risti*, Öpir ristade. Foto: Berig, [CC BY 2.5](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_104,_Ed.jpg).

:::box Så säkra är vi
Ett mönster i ett stort material kan uppstå av en slump, eller av att materialet är skevt. Därför har vi prövat det på flera sätt:

- **Samma ristare, samma trakt.** Modellen jämför stenar av samma ristare och i samma område. Ökningen är alltså inte bara en skillnad mellan ristare eller mellan landskap.
- **Många test på en gång.** Vi prövade 14 drag samtidigt och justerade för det (Holms metod). Signaturens ökning klarar justeringen (justerat p 0,002): ett så tydligt mönster skulle uppstå av en slump bland de 14 dragen i färre än ett fall på 500.
- **Två oberoende halvor.** Vi delade stenarna i två grupper, socken för socken, så att båda grupperna fick stenar från samma trakter och ungefär samma tid, och gjorde om hela analysen i varje grupp för sig. Mönstret syns i båda: från 7 till 28 % i den ena och från 1 till 24 % i den andra. Hade det bara funnits i den ena hade det kunnat bero på några enskilda socknar eller ristare.
- **Osäkra årtal.** Stilgruppernas dateringar är ungefärliga. Vi räknade om tio gånger med årtal lottade inom varje stilgrupps intervall, och alla tio gav en tydlig ökning, mellan 13 och 21 procentenheter.
- **Vår sökning och Rundatas.** Vi hittar signaturer genom att söka efter ristarformler (*risti*, *hiogg*, *markaði* …) och kan missa ovanliga former. Rundatas egen uppgift om vilka stenar som är signerade ger samma bild: från 4 % i RAK till 38 % i Pr5.
:::

## Vår hypotes – och två prövningar

Att ristarna signerar allt oftare är känt, särskilt i Uppland, och Magnus Källström har undersökt signaturerna grundligt (2007). Det vi tillför är mätningen med ristare och trakt konstanta, och iakttagelsen att signaturen tar över textens sista plats samtidigt som bönen lämnar den. Det kräver en förklaring.

Den närmaste förklaringen är att runristningen blev ett yrke: ristare med många uppdrag satte sitt namn på verket, som en mästares märke – kanske som reklam. Den förklaringen har två följder som går att pröva.

**Trängde signaturen undan bönen?** Om ristarens namn ersatte bönen som textens avslutning, borde en sten med en bön sällan ha en signatur – de skulle tävla om samma plats. Vi jämförde stenar inom samma stilgrupp (804 daterade stenar). En sten med en bön var lika ofta signerad som en sten utan bön från samma tid. Oddskvoten är 1,1, alltså i praktiken ingen skillnad, och den ligger sannolikt mellan 0,6 och 1,9 (p 0,69: en skillnad av den storleken uppstår lätt av en slump). Bönen och signaturen valdes var för sig. Det sista ordet bytte ägare för att bönerna blev färre och signaturerna fler, inte för att det ena trängde undan det andra.

**Följde signaturen efterfrågan?** Om signaturen var en mästares reklam borde den vara vanligast där det restes många stenar, för där fanns flest beställare och flest ristare att konkurrera med. Vi räknade hur många runstenar som står inom en mil från varje sten och delade stenarna i tre lika stora grupper, från de glesaste trakterna (högst 22 stenar inom en mil) till de tätaste (fler än 55). I de senare stilgrupperna, Pr3 till Pr5, när signaturen var vanlig, är andelen signerade stenar nästan densamma i alla tre: 25, 24 och 24 %. I en modell med stilgrupp och landskap finns inget samband (p 0,29). Signaturen var inte vanligare där marknaden var störst.

**Den följde ristarna.** Det som skiljer är ristaren. Öpir satte sitt namn på 38 % av de stenar vi kan läsa, Balle på 37 % och Åsmund på 27 %. Fot, som var verksam vid samma tid och också har många stenar, signerade 10 %, och Gunnar, en av de tidiga ristarna, 3 %. Att ha många uppdrag ledde alltså inte av sig självt till en signatur. Det var något somliga ristare gjorde och andra inte.

Vi formulerar därför hypotesen skarpare:

> Signaturen spreds som en sed mellan ristarna – från mästare till lärjunge och mellan ristare som arbetade sida vid sida – inte som svar på beställarnas efterfrågan.

Prövningarna har sina gränser: antalet stenar inom en mil är ett grovt mått på efterfrågan, och stilgrupperna delar in tiden i steg om ungefär tjugofem år.

## Så kan hypotesen prövas vidare

1. **Ristarnas nätverk.** Om signaturen gick i arv mellan ristare borde ristare som samarbetade eller lärde av varandra signera ungefär lika ofta, oberoende av var de verkade.
2. **Signaturens ord.** Formlerna varierar – *risti*, *hiogg*, *markaði* – och ibland följer ett beröm, som i Balles uppmaning till den runkunnige. Spreds en sed bör formuleringarna följa ristarnas skolor snarare än landskapen.
3. **Ristarens egen bana.** Var signerandet något en ristare lärde sig eller växte in i, kan andelen signerade stenar öka under en och samma ristares verksamhet. Det kräver att varje ristares stenar dateras finare än stilgrupperna medger.
4. **De påkostade stenarna.** Var signaturen ett försäljningsargument trots allt, borde den vara vanligare på de största och mest påkostade stenarna. Stenarnas mått finns för en del av materialet.

## Förbehåll

- Dateringen bygger på ornamentiken och är ungefärlig, och stilgrupperna är utarbetade för stenarna i Uppland och Södermanland.
- Signaturerna hittas genom att söka efter ristarformler i Rundatas normaliserade text, och en skadad text kan dölja en signatur. Därför följer vi textens slut bara på stenar där slutet är bevarat.
- Många ristare är kända just genom sina signaturer, och osignerade stenar har tillskrivits dem efter stilen. Andelen signerade stenar per ristare vilar därför på forskarnas attributioner.
- Den sista stilgruppen, Pr5, består till stor del av Öpirs stenar.
- Ett samband i tid är inte en orsak. Hypotesen förklarar mönstret, men andra förklaringar är möjliga – till exempel att fler kunde läsa, så att ett namn på stenen fick fler läsare.

:::box Det viktigaste i korthet
- På de tidigaste runstenarna nämns ristaren nästan aldrig; på de sista står hans namn på mer än var tredje sten, nästan alltid allra sist – efter Gud.
- Det sista ordet i texterna byter ägare under 1000-talet: omkring 1035 var det oftast en bön, femtio år senare oftast ristarens namn.
- Signaturen trängde inte undan bönen, och den följde inte efterfrågan – den följde ristarna: somliga signerade var tredje sten, andra nästan aldrig.
- Vår hypotes att pröva: signaturen spreds som en sed från mästare till lärjunge – ett tidigt exempel på hur hantverkare blev upphovsmän.
:::

## Se själv

![Ristarsignatur på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050](/figurer/501e268b953fc9fb.webp)
Ristarsignatur på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050. Källa: Vitkis mönsterkarta (r/blogfig.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

![Kristen bön på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050](/figurer/b873bbd714cc368f.webp)
Kristen bön på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050. Källa: Vitkis mönsterkarta (r/blogfig.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

![Förändringsmodellens kurvor: kristen bön, kors och ristarsignatur](/figurer/b21d76714e9e547b.webp)
Förändringsmodellens kurvor: kristen bön, kors och ristarsignatur. Källa: Vitkis korpusanalys i R (change.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

Om hur bönen lämnade stenarna: [Bönen tystnade – men korset stod kvar](/artiklar/2026-10-bonen-tystnade-korset-stod-kvar).

Kartorna, kurvorna och modellerna kommer från Vitki, ett öppet verktyg för runstensforskning som du kan ladda ner och köra på din egen dator från [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes). Metoden beskrivs i [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md).

## Källor och data

- Samnordisk runtextdatabas (Rundata), Institutionen för nordiska språk, Uppsala universitet. Open Database License.
- Gräslund, A.-S. 2006. Dating the Swedish Viking-Age rune stones on stylistic grounds. I: M. Stoklund m.fl. (red.), *Runes and their Secrets: Studies in Runology*. Köpenhamn: Museum Tusculanum Press, s. 117–139.
- Källström, M. 2007. *Mästare och minnesmärken. Studier kring vikingatida runristare och skriftmiljöer i Norden*. Stockholm Studies in Scandinavian Philology, New Series 43. Stockholm: Stockholms universitet.
- Holm, S. 1979. A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics* 6, s. 65–70.
- Wood, S. N. 2017. *Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R*. 2:a uppl. Boca Raton: CRC Press.
- Foton: Wikimedia Commons, med fotograf och licens i bildtexterna.
posts.title_en: The carver had the last word
posts.summary_en: Around 1035 more than one runestone in four ended with a prayer to God. Fifty years later more of them ended with the carver's own name. But the signature did not push the prayer aside, and it did not follow demand – it followed the carvers. We think it spread as a custom from master to apprentice.
posts.body_en:
*Viðhugsi had this stone raised in memory of his good father. He lived in Ågersta. Here the stone shall stand between the farms. May the man who is skilled in runes interpret the runes that Balli carved.*

So it reads on a runestone at Ågersta in Uppland, carved some time between 1050 and 1080 to judge by its ornament. The father's name can be interpreted in two ways, but there is no doubt about the carver: Balli puts his name last, after a challenge to anyone who can read. He was not alone. On the earliest runestones the carver is almost never named, but on the last ones the carver's name stands on more than one stone in three, and nearly always at the very end. The last word, which a generation earlier was often a prayer to God, became the carver's.

![The runestone U 729](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg/960px-U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg)
U 729 at Ågersta in Uppland, carved by Balli. The text ends with *the runes that Balli carved*. Photo: Bengt A. Lundberg, [CC BY 2.5 SE](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5/se/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg).

:::box In short
- The carver's name – the signature – stands on 3 % of the earliest runestones and on 38 % of the last ones, nearly always at the end of the text.
- Around 1035 more texts ended with a prayer than with the carver's name. Fifty years later it was the other way round: the last word had passed from God to the carver.
- But the signature did not push the prayer off the stones, and it was not more common where many stones were raised. It followed the carvers: some signed one stone in three, others almost never.
- Our hypothesis: the signature spread as a custom among the carvers, from master to apprentice, not in answer to the patrons' demand. It can be tested.
:::

## The last word changes hands

We went through the 1,292 runestones in Sweden that have a legible text in the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base. On 182 of them the carver wrote his name, with a carver's formula such as *Balli risti*, Balli carved. Nine signatures in ten stand among the last five words of the text. The prayer – *God help his soul* – usually comes last as well. And on the 36 stones that have both a prayer and a signature, the signature comes after the prayer, on every single one. The carver has the last word, after God.

So we can follow how the texts end. 740 of the dated stones have a surviving ending.

:::chart How the text ends, by style group
# With a prayer
RAK, around 1000 | 10 | 155 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 23 | 137 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 19 | 47 stones
+Pr2, around 1035 | 27 | 81 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 22 | 111 stones
Pr4, around 1085 | 7 | 180 stones
Pr5, around 1115 | 3 | 29 stones
# With the carver's name
RAK, around 1000 | 2 | 155 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 7 | 137 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 13 | 47 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 12 | 81 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 22 | 111 stones
+Pr4, around 1085 | 22 | 180 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 38 | 29 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis of the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base; stones whose ending survives, dated by their style group (Gräslund 2006).
:::

Around 1035, in the style group Pr2, 27 % of the texts end with a prayer and 12 % with the carver's name. A generation later, in Pr3, they are equally common, 22 % each. In Pr4, around 1085, the balance has turned: 7 % end with a prayer and 22 % with the carver's name. Among the last runestones, in Pr5, 38 % end with the carver's name and 3 % with a prayer.

## The signature spreads

Counting all dated stones, not only those with a surviving ending, the carver's name stands on 3 % of the earliest (RAK) and on 38 % of the last (Pr5).

:::chart Share of runestones with the carver's name, by style group
+RAK, around 1000 | 3 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 7 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 16 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 13 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 23 | 118 stones
Pr4, around 1085 | 23 | 198 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 38 | 32 stones
Source: as above, all dated stones with a legible text.
:::

Our model compares stones by the same carver and in the same area. With it the share rises from about 6 per cent around the year 1000 to 28 per cent in the early 1100s – an increase of 22 percentage points, probably somewhere between 10 and 36.

The last bar needs an explanation. 28 of the 32 stones in Pr5 were carved by one and the same carver, Œpir, who signed about one stone in three that he made. That bar is therefore largely his. But the increase is not down to him: without Œpir's stones the share rises from 3 % in RAK to 23 % in Pr3 and 19 % in Pr4.

![The runestone U 104](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/U_104%2C_Ed.jpg/960px-U_104%2C_Ed.jpg)
U 104 at Ed church in Uppland, one of Œpir's stones. The text ends *ØpiR risti*, Œpir carved. Photo: Berig, [CC BY 2.5](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_104,_Ed.jpg).

:::box How sure we are
A pattern in a large material can arise by chance, or because the material is skewed. So we have tested it in several ways:

- **Same carver, same area.** The model compares stones by the same carver and in the same area. The increase is therefore not just a difference between carvers or between provinces.
- **Many tests at once.** We tested 14 features at the same time and adjusted for it (Holm's method). The rise of the signature survives the adjustment (adjusted p 0.002): a pattern this clear would arise by chance among the 14 features in fewer than one case in 500.
- **Two independent halves.** We split the stones into two groups, parish by parish, so that both groups got stones from the same districts and about the same time, and redid the whole analysis in each group on its own. The pattern shows in both: from 7 to 28 % in one and from 1 to 24 % in the other. Had it been found in only one, it could have been down to a few particular parishes or carvers.
- **Uncertain years.** The style groups' dates are approximate. We recalculated ten times with years drawn at random within each group's interval, and all ten gave a clear increase, between 13 and 21 percentage points.
- **Our search and Rundata's.** We find signatures by searching for carver's formulas (*risti*, *hiogg*, *markaði* …) and may miss rare forms. Rundata's own record of which stones are signed gives the same picture: from 4 % in RAK to 38 % in Pr5.
:::

## Our hypothesis – and two tests

That carvers sign more and more often is known, especially in Uppland, and Magnus Källström has studied the signatures thoroughly (2007). What we add is the measurement with carver and area held constant, and the observation that the signature takes over the last place in the text just as the prayer leaves it. That calls for an explanation.

The nearest explanation is that rune carving became a trade: carvers with many commissions put their name on the work, as a master's mark – perhaps as advertising. That explanation has two consequences that can be tested.

**Did the signature push the prayer aside?** If the carver's name replaced the prayer as the ending of the text, a stone with a prayer should rarely have a signature – they would compete for the same place. We compared stones within the same style group (804 dated stones). A stone with a prayer was signed just as often as a stone without one from the same time. The odds ratio is 1.1, in practice no difference, and it probably lies between 0.6 and 1.9 (p 0.69: a difference of that size easily arises by chance). The prayer and the signature were chosen separately. The last word changed hands because prayers became fewer and signatures more frequent, not because one pushed the other aside.

**Did the signature follow demand?** If the signature was a master's advertisement, it should be most common where many stones were raised, for there were the most patrons and the most carvers to compete with. We counted how many runestones stand within ten kilometres of each stone and split the stones into three equal groups, from the sparsest districts (at most 22 stones within ten kilometres) to the densest (more than 55). In the later style groups, Pr3 to Pr5, when the signature was common, the share of signed stones is almost the same in all three: 25, 24 and 24 %. In a model with style group and province there is no association (p 0.29). The signature was not more common where the market was largest.

**It followed the carvers.** What makes the difference is the carver. Œpir put his name on 38 % of the stones we can read, Balli on 37 % and Ásmundr on 27 %. Fótr, who was active at the same time and also has many stones, signed 10 %, and Gunnarr, one of the early carvers, 3 %. Having many commissions did not by itself lead to a signature. It was something some carvers did and others did not.

So we state the hypothesis more sharply:

> The signature spread as a custom among the carvers – from master to apprentice and between carvers who worked side by side – not in answer to the patrons' demand.

The tests have their limits: the number of stones within ten kilometres is a rough measure of demand, and the style groups divide time into steps of about twenty-five years.

## How the hypothesis can be tested further

1. **The carvers' network.** If the signature was passed on between carvers, carvers who worked together or learnt from each other should sign about equally often, wherever they worked.
2. **The words of the signature.** The formulas vary – *risti*, *hiogg*, *markaði* – and sometimes praise follows, as in Balli's challenge to the rune-skilled. If a custom spread, the wording should follow the carvers' schools rather than the provinces.
3. **The carver's own career.** If signing was something a carver learnt or grew into, the share of signed stones may rise within one carver's career. That requires each carver's stones to be dated more finely than the style groups allow.
4. **The costly stones.** If the signature was a selling point after all, it should be more common on the largest and most elaborate stones. The stones' measurements exist for part of the material.

## Caveats

- The dating rests on the ornament and is approximate, and the style groups were worked out for the stones of Uppland and Södermanland.
- Signatures are found by searching for carver's formulas in Rundata's normalised text, and a damaged text can hide a signature. So we follow the ending of the text only on stones whose ending survives.
- Many carvers are known precisely through their signatures, and unsigned stones have been attributed to them by style. The share of signed stones per carver therefore rests on the scholars' attributions.
- The last style group, Pr5, consists largely of Œpir's stones.
- An association in time is not a cause. The hypothesis explains the pattern, but other explanations are possible – for example that more people could read, so that a name on the stone found more readers.

:::box The essentials in brief
- On the earliest runestones the carver is almost never named; on the last ones his name stands on more than every third stone, almost always last – after God.
- The final word of the texts changes owner during the eleventh century: around 1035 it was usually a prayer, fifty years later usually the carver's name.
- The signature did not displace the prayer, and it did not follow demand – it followed the carvers: some signed every third stone, others almost never.
- Our hypothesis to test: the signature spread as a custom from master to apprentice – an early example of craftsmen becoming authors.
:::

## See for yourself

![Carver's signature on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050](/figurer/4b3f3c713193e9ea.webp)
Carver's signature on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050. Source: Vitki's pattern map (r/blogfig.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

![Christian prayer on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050](/figurer/ac99d4ae73b5032f.webp)
Christian prayer on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050. Source: Vitki's pattern map (r/blogfig.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

![The change model's curves: Christian prayer, cross and carver's signature](/figurer/c66cb50dcf72ce3e.webp)
The change model's curves: Christian prayer, cross and carver's signature. Source: Vitki's corpus analysis in R (change.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

On how the prayer left the stones: [The prayer fell silent – but the cross remained](/artiklar/2026-10-bonen-tystnade-korset-stod-kvar).

The maps, curves and models come from Vitki, an open tool for runestone research that you can download and run on your own computer from [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes). The method is described in [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md).

## Sources and data

- Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (Rundata), Department of Scandinavian Languages, Uppsala University. Open Database License.
- Gräslund, A.-S. 2006. Dating the Swedish Viking-Age rune stones on stylistic grounds. In: M. Stoklund et al. (eds), *Runes and their Secrets: Studies in Runology*. Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum Press, pp. 117–139.
- Källström, M. 2007. *Mästare och minnesmärken. Studier kring vikingatida runristare och skriftmiljöer i Norden*. Stockholm Studies in Scandinavian Philology, New Series 43. Stockholm: Stockholm University.
- Holm, S. 1979. A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics* 6, pp. 65–70.
- Wood, S. N. 2017. *Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R*. 2nd edn. Boca Raton: CRC Press.
- Photos: Wikimedia Commons, with photographer and licence in the captions.

posts.title: Bönen tystnade – men korset stod kvar
posts.summary: Omkring år 1035 bad mer än var tredje runsten Gud om hjälp för den dödes själ. Femtio år senare gjorde bara en av tio det, fast korset fanns kvar på stenarna. Vi tror att bönen inte försvann – den flyttade in i kyrkan.
posts.body:
*Tova och Häming lät resa denna sten efter Gunnar, sin son. Han dog ute bland grekerna. Gud hjälpe hans själ och Guds moder.*

Så står det på en runsten vid Åshusby i Uppland, ristad någon gång mellan 1020 och 1050 att döma av ornamentiken och tillskriven ristaren Åsmund. Den sista meningen är en bön, och den är inte ovanlig: ungefär var femte runsten med läsbar text ber Gud, Kristus eller Guds moder att hjälpa den döde. Men när vi följde bönen genom tiden såg vi något som förvånade oss. Bönen kommer och går – medan korset stannar.

![Runstenen U 431](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG/960px-U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG)
U 431 vid Åshusby i Uppland. Bönen – *Gud hjälpe hans själ och Guds moder* – står sist i texten. Foto: Berig, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_431,_%C3%85shusby.JPG).

:::box Kort sagt
- Kristna böner på runstenar var vanligast under 1030- och 1040-talen och nästan borta i början av 1100-talet.
- Korset finns kvar på en stor del av stenarna, omkring sex av tio i de sena stilgrupperna. Det var inte kristendomen som försvann, utan bönen.
- Samtidigt blir det allt vanligare att ristaren skriver sitt namn på stenen.
- Vår hypotes: bönen tystnade när förbönen för de döda blev kyrkans sak. Den kan prövas.
:::

## Bönen kommer – och går

Vi gick igenom de 1 292 runstenar i Sverige som har en läsbar text i Samnordisk runtextdatabas och letade efter böner: *Gud hjälpe hans själ*, *Gud hjälpe hans ande*, *Guds moder* och deras många stavningar. 804 av stenarna kan dateras ungefär genom sin ornamentik. Runstenskonsten bytte stil under 1000-talet, och forskarna har ordnat stilarna i en följd, från RAK omkring år 1000 till Pr5 i början av 1100-talet.

:::chart Andel runstenar med kristen bön, efter stilgrupp
RAK, omkring 1000 | 15 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 28 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 24 | 51 stenar
+Pr2, omkring 1035 | 37 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 29 | 118 stenar
Pr4, omkring 1085 | 10 | 198 stenar
Pr5, omkring 1115 | 3 | 32 stenar
Källa: Vitkis korpusanalys av Samnordisk runtextdatabas; stenarna är daterade efter sin stilgrupp (Gräslund 2006).
:::

Bönen blir vanligare under 1000-talets första hälft och når sin topp med stilgruppen Pr2, omkring 1035, då 37 % av stenarna bär en bön. Sedan faller den brant: 10 % i Pr4 och 3 % i Pr5, bland de sista runstenarna. Vår modell, som tar hänsyn till vem som ristade stenen och var den står, lägger toppen omkring 1038 (mellan 1023 och 1048) och visar en nedgång från omkring 30 till 2 procent i början av 1100-talet.

## Det var inte tron som försvann

Man kunde tro att bönen försvinner för att stenarna blir mindre kristna. Korset talar emot det. Det finns på 46 % av de tidigaste stenarna, på 70 % omkring 1035 och fortfarande på 62 % i Pr4 och Pr5, långt efter att bönen har börjat tystna. Med samma modell som för bönen minskar visserligen också korset efter toppen omkring 1028, från omkring 70 till 40 procent, men den minskningen håller inte i båda halvorna av materialet. Bönen faller till en femtondel; korset finns kvar på en stor del av stenarna. Det är bönen, uppmaningen till Gud att hjälpa den döde, som nästan försvinner.

:::chart Korset och ristarens namn på samma stenar
# Kors
RAK, omkring 1000 | 46 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 68 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 76 | 51 stenar
Pr2, omkring 1035 | 70 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 63 | 118 stenar
+Pr4, omkring 1085 | 62 | 198 stenar
+Pr5, omkring 1115 | 62 | 32 stenar
# Ristarens signatur
RAK, omkring 1000 | 3 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 7 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 16 | 51 stenar
Pr2, omkring 1035 | 13 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 23 | 118 stenar
+Pr4, omkring 1085 | 23 | 198 stenar
+Pr5, omkring 1115 | 38 | 32 stenar
Källa: som ovan.
:::

Samtidigt händer något annat: ristarna börjar signera. På de tidigaste stenarna står ristarens namn på 3 %, på de sista på 38 %. *Öpir ristade*, står det på stenen vid Morby i Uppland, där en mor lät bygga en bro för sin dotters själ – utan en bön.

![Runstenen U 489](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/U_489%2C_Morby.jpg/960px-U_489%2C_Morby.jpg)
U 489 vid Morby i Uppland, ristad av Öpir under stilgruppen Pr4: en bro för en dotters själ, ristarens namn – men ingen bön. Foto: Christine Jewell from Canada, [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_489,_Morby.jpg).

:::box Så säkra är vi
Ett mönster i ett stort material kan uppstå av en slump, eller av att materialet är skevt. Därför har vi prövat det på flera sätt:

- **Samma ristare, samma trakt.** Modellen jämför stenar som har ristats av samma ristare och står i samma område. Nedgången är alltså inte bara en enskild ristares vana eller en skillnad mellan landskap.
- **Många test på en gång.** Vi prövade 14 drag samtidigt och justerade för det (Holms metod). Bönens förändring klarar justeringen med god marginal (justerat p under 0,001): ett så tydligt mönster skulle uppstå av en slump bland de 14 dragen i mindre än ett fall på tusen.
- **Två oberoende halvor.** Vi delade stenarna i två grupper, socken för socken, så att båda grupperna fick stenar från samma trakter och ungefär samma tid, och gjorde om hela analysen i varje grupp för sig. Mönstret syns i båda. Hade det bara funnits i den ena hade det kunnat bero på några enskilda socknar eller ristare.
- **Osäkra årtal.** Stilgruppernas dateringar är ungefärliga. Vi räknade om tio gånger med årtal lottade inom varje stilgrupps intervall, och alla tio gav samma resultat.
- **Skadade stenar.** Bönen står oftast sist i texten, där många stenar är skadade. Med bara de stenar vars slut är bevarat består nedgången.
- **Vår egen sökning.** Inför inlägget kontrollerade vi sökningen efter böner och hittade stavningar den missade, som *hiælpi* och *hialpin*. Siffrorna här bygger på den rättade sökningen.
:::

## Vår hypotes: bönen flyttade in i kyrkan

Att runstenar bär böner är välkänt, och forskningen har länge sett runstenarna som en del av kristnandet. Det vi tillför är mätningen: att bönens uppgång och fall går att följa med ristare och trakt konstanta, och att den skiljer sig från korset, som består. Det kräver en förklaring.

Vår hypotes är att bönen på stenen var lekfolkets egen förbön under missionstiden. Under 1000-talets första hälft fanns ännu få kyrkor och präster i Mälardalen. Den som ville att någon skulle be för den dödes själ kunde sätta bönen där den syntes – på stenen vid vägen, kanske i hopp om att förbipasserande skulle be. När kyrkan växte fram under 1000-talets andra hälft, med präster, vigd jord och mässor för de döda, blev förbönen kyrkans uppgift. Stenen behövde inte längre be. Den fortsatte att bära korset, som ett tecken för tron och släkten, och blev alltmer ett minnesmärke – signerat av sin ristare.

## En första prövning: ett skifte samtidigt överallt

Om det var den lokala kyrkan som gjorde stenens bön överflödig, borde bönen tystna tidigare där kyrkorna kom tidigt. Det kunde vi pröva. Vi tog de medeltida kyrkor i Wikidata som är uppförda senast år 1200 och jämförde stenar nära och långt från dem, bara stenar som står kvar på sin ursprungliga plats (504 daterade stenar).

Resultatet var tydligt, men inte det vi väntade oss. Bönen är något vanligare nära de tidiga kyrkorna, men den tystnar lika snabbt överallt: efter omkring 1075 bär 4 % av stenarna inom tre kilometer från en tidig kyrka en bön (25 stenar), och 3 % av dem längre bort (118 stenar). Vi ser inget tecken på att bönen försvann tidigare nära kyrkorna (p 0,28 för skillnaden i hur snabbt den försvinner).

Det talar emot den enklaste formen av hypotesen – att varje gård slutade be på sin sten när den fick sin kyrka – och för ett gemensamt skifte som slog igenom ungefär samtidigt i hela Mälardalen. Ett sådant skifte kunde komma uppifrån: under 1000-talets andra hälft började kyrkan organiseras i stift, och Sigtuna nämns som biskopssäte omkring 1060. Vi formulerar därför hypotesen skarpare:

> Bönen tystnade när förbönen för de döda blev en sak för den organiserade kyrkan, inte för den enskilda släkten.

Prövningen har en gräns: stilgrupperna delar in tiden i steg om ungefär tjugofem år, så en skillnad på något decennium skulle inte synas.

## Så kan hypotesen prövas vidare

1. **Finare datering.** Om ristarnas verksamhet dateras finare, genom ristarnas samarbeten och kedjor av lärare och elever, går det att se om bönen tystnar samtidigt överallt eller om skiftet sprider sig från stiftens centra.
2. **Bönens ord.** Om kyrkan tog över förbönen bör bönernas ordval närma sig kyrkans språk innan de försvinner. Guds moder nämns i 27 % av bönerna i Pr2 och 25 % i Pr3, mot 12 % i RAK och 5 % i Pr4 – ett spår att följa, även om antalet böner per stilgrupp är litet.
3. **Andra landskap och länder.** Där kyrkan organiserades tidigare eller senare bör bönen ha tystnat tidigare respektive senare. En jämförelse med Danmark kräver bättre uppgifter om korsen på de danska stenarna än vi har i dag.
4. **Gåvor för själen.** Om förbönen flyttade in i kyrkan kan gåvor för den dödes själ – till kyrkan eller i form av broar – ha tagit bönens plats. Brobyggen ökar inte tydligt i vårt material, och gåvor till kyrkan syns inte på stenarna; här behövs andra källor.

## Förbehåll

- Dateringen bygger på ornamentiken och är ungefärlig, och stilgrupperna är utarbetade för stenarna i Uppland och Södermanland.
- Böner hittas genom att söka i Rundatas normaliserade text. En skadad text kan dölja en bön; därför prövade vi stenar med bevarat slut för sig.
- Ett samband i tid är inte en orsak. Hypotesen förklarar mönstret, men andra förklaringar är möjliga – till exempel att en ny generation ristare hade andra ideal. Att mönstret håller med ristaren konstant talar dock emot att det bara är ett generationsskifte.
- Under arbetet hittade vi också ett fel i hur appen räknar bort stenar som har flyttats till kyrkor. Det påverkar inte huvudfyndet, som inte bygger på var stenarna står, men prövningen mot de tidiga kyrkorna är gjord med det rättade urvalet. Felet har rättats i appen och beskrivs i metodbeskrivningen.

:::box Det viktigaste i korthet
- Omkring 1035 bad mer än var tredje daterad runsten Gud om hjälp för den dödes själ. Femtio år senare gjorde nästan ingen det.
- Det var inte tron som försvann: korset står kvar på en stor del av de sena stenarna. Det var just bönen som tystnade.
- Samtidigt tog ristarens namn bönens plats sist i texterna.
- Vår hypotes att pröva: bönen försvann från stenarna när förbönen för de döda blev kyrkans sak – minnet stannade på stenen, omsorgen om själen flyttade in i kyrkan.
:::

## Se själv

Kristen bön på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050. Källa: Vitkis mönsterkarta (r/blogfig.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

![Ristarsignatur på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050](/figurer/501e268b953fc9fb.webp)
Ristarsignatur på Vitkis mönsterkarta, före och efter omkring 1050. Källa: Vitkis mönsterkarta (r/blogfig.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

![Förändringsmodellens kurvor: kristen bön, kors och ristarsignatur](/figurer/b21d76714e9e547b.webp)
Förändringsmodellens kurvor: kristen bön, kors och ristarsignatur. Källa: Vitkis korpusanalys i R (change.R); Samnordisk runtextdatabas (ODbL).

Kartorna, kurvorna och modellerna kommer från Vitki, ett öppet verktyg för runstensforskning som du kan ladda ner och köra på din egen dator från [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes). Metoden beskrivs i [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md).

## Källor och data

- Samnordisk runtextdatabas (Rundata), Institutionen för nordiska språk, Uppsala universitet. Open Database License.
- Gräslund, A.-S. 2006. Dating the Swedish Viking-Age rune stones on stylistic grounds. I: M. Stoklund m.fl. (red.), *Runes and their Secrets: Studies in Runology*. Köpenhamn: Museum Tusculanum Press, s. 117–139.
- Sawyer, B. 2000. *The Viking-Age Rune-Stones: Custom and Commemoration in Early Medieval Scandinavia*. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
- Holm, S. 1979. A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics* 6, s. 65–70.
- Wood, S. N. 2017. *Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R*. 2:a uppl. Boca Raton: CRC Press.
- Medeltida kyrkor: Wikidata (CC0). Foton: Wikimedia Commons, med fotograf och licens i bildtexterna.
posts.title_en: The prayer fell silent – but the cross remained
posts.summary_en: Around the year 1035 more than one runestone in three asked God to help the soul of the dead. Fifty years later only one in ten did, although the cross remained on the stones. We think the prayer did not disappear – it moved into the church.
posts.body_en:
*Tófa and Hemingr had this stone raised in memory of Gunnarr, their son. He died abroad among the Greeks. May God and God's mother help his soul.*

So reads a runestone at Åshusby in Uppland, carved some time between 1020 and 1050 to judge by its ornament and attributed to the carver Åsmundr. The last sentence is a prayer, and it is not unusual: about one in five runestones with a legible text asks God, Christ or God's mother to help the dead. But when we followed the prayer through time we saw something that surprised us. The prayer comes and goes – while the cross stays.

![The runestone U 431](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG/960px-U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG)
U 431 at Åshusby in Uppland. The prayer – *May God and God's mother help his soul* – comes last in the text. Photo: Berig, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_431,_%C3%85shusby.JPG).

:::box In short
- Christian prayers on runestones were most common in the 1030s and 1040s and almost gone by the early 1100s.
- The cross remains on a large share of the stones, about six in ten in the late style groups. It was not Christianity that disappeared, but the prayer.
- At the same time it becomes ever more common for the carver to sign the stone.
- Our hypothesis: the prayer fell silent when intercession for the dead became the church's task. It can be tested.
:::

## The prayer comes – and goes

We went through the 1,292 runestones in Sweden that have a legible text in the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base and looked for prayers: *God help his soul*, *God help his spirit*, *God's mother* and their many spellings. 804 of the stones can be roughly dated by their ornament. Runestone art changed style during the eleventh century, and scholars have put the styles in order, from RAK around the year 1000 to Pr5 in the early 1100s.

:::chart Share of runestones with a Christian prayer, by style group
RAK, around 1000 | 15 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 28 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 24 | 51 stones
+Pr2, around 1035 | 37 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 29 | 118 stones
Pr4, around 1085 | 10 | 198 stones
Pr5, around 1115 | 3 | 32 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis of the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base; stones dated by their style group (Gräslund 2006).
:::

The prayer becomes more common in the first half of the eleventh century and peaks with the style group Pr2, around 1035, when 37 % of the stones carry a prayer. Then it falls steeply: 10 % in Pr4 and 3 % in Pr5, among the last runestones. Our model, which takes into account who carved the stone and where it stands, puts the peak around 1038 (between 1023 and 1048) and shows a decline from about 30 to 2 per cent in the early 1100s.

## It was not the faith that disappeared

One might think that the prayer disappears because the stones become less Christian. The cross speaks against that. It is found on 46 % of the earliest stones, on 70 % around 1035 and still on 62 % in Pr4 and Pr5, long after the prayer has begun to fall silent. With the same model as for the prayer the cross does decline after its peak around 1028, from about 70 to 40 per cent, but that decline does not hold in both halves of the material. The prayer falls to a fifteenth; the cross remains on a large share of the stones. It is the prayer, the plea to God to help the dead, that almost disappears.

:::chart The cross and the carver's name on the same stones
# Cross
RAK, around 1000 | 46 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 68 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 76 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 70 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 63 | 118 stones
+Pr4, around 1085 | 62 | 198 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 62 | 32 stones
# Carver's signature
RAK, around 1000 | 3 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 7 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 16 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 13 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 23 | 118 stones
+Pr4, around 1085 | 23 | 198 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 38 | 32 stones
Source: as above.
:::

At the same time something else happens: the carvers begin to sign. The carver's name appears on 3 % of the earliest stones and on 38 % of the last. *Œpir carved*, says the stone at Morby in Uppland, where a mother had a bridge built for her daughter's soul – without a prayer.

![The runestone U 489](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/U_489%2C_Morby.jpg/960px-U_489%2C_Morby.jpg)
U 489 at Morby in Uppland, carved by Œpir in style group Pr4: a bridge for a daughter's soul, the carver's name – but no prayer. Photo: Christine Jewell from Canada, [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_489,_Morby.jpg).

:::box How sure we are
A pattern in a large material can arise by chance, or because the material is skewed. So we have tested it in several ways:

- **Same carver, same area.** The model compares stones carved by the same carver and standing in the same area. The decline is therefore not just one carver's habit or a difference between provinces.
- **Many tests at once.** We tested 14 features at the same time and adjusted for it (Holm's method). The change in the prayer passes the adjustment with a good margin (adjusted p below 0.001): a pattern this clear would arise by chance among the 14 features in fewer than one case in a thousand.
- **Two independent halves.** We split the stones into two groups, parish by parish, so that both groups got stones from the same districts and about the same time, and redid the whole analysis in each group on its own. The pattern appears in both. Had it been found in only one, it could have been down to a few particular parishes or carvers.
- **Uncertain years.** The style groups' dates are approximate. We recalculated ten times with years drawn at random within each style group's interval, and all ten gave the same result.
- **Damaged stones.** The prayer usually comes last in the text, where many stones are damaged. With only the stones whose end is preserved, the decline remains.
- **Our own search.** Before writing this post we checked the search for prayers and found spellings it missed, such as *hiælpi* and *hialpin*. The figures here use the corrected search.
:::

## Our hypothesis: the prayer moved into the church

That runestones carry prayers is well known, and scholars have long seen the runestones as part of the conversion. What we add is the measurement: the rise and fall of the prayer can be followed with carver and area held constant, and it differs from the cross, which remains. That calls for an explanation.

Our hypothesis is that the prayer on the stone was the laity's own intercession during the mission period. In the first half of the eleventh century there were still few churches and priests in the Mälaren valley. Whoever wanted someone to pray for the soul of the dead could put the prayer where it was seen – on the stone by the road, perhaps in the hope that passers-by would pray. When the church grew in the second half of the century, with priests, consecrated ground and masses for the dead, intercession became the church's task. The stone no longer needed to pray. It went on carrying the cross, as a sign of faith and family, and increasingly became a memorial – signed by its carver.

## A first test: a shift at the same time everywhere

If it was the local church that made the stone's prayer superfluous, the prayer should fall silent earlier where churches came early. That we could test. We took the medieval churches in Wikidata built by the year 1200 and compared stones near and far from them, using only stones still standing where they were raised (504 dated stones).

The result was clear, but not what we expected. The prayer is somewhat more common near the early churches, but it falls silent just as fast everywhere: after about 1075, 4 % of the stones within three kilometres of an early church carry a prayer (25 stones), and 3 % of those further away (118 stones). We see no sign that the prayer disappeared earlier near the churches (p 0.28 for the difference in how fast it disappears).

That speaks against the simplest form of the hypothesis – that each farm stopped praying on its stone when it got its church – and for a common shift that took hold at about the same time throughout the Mälaren valley. Such a shift could come from above: in the second half of the eleventh century the church began to be organised in dioceses, and Sigtuna is mentioned as a bishop's seat around 1060. We therefore state the hypothesis more sharply:

> The prayer fell silent when intercession for the dead became a matter for the organised church, not for the individual family.

The test has a limit: the style groups divide time into steps of about twenty-five years, so a difference of a decade or so would not show.

## How the hypothesis can be tested further

1. **Finer dating.** If the carvers' careers are dated more finely, through their collaborations and chains of masters and pupils, it can be seen whether the prayer falls silent at the same time everywhere or whether the shift spreads from the centres of the dioceses.
2. **The words of the prayer.** If the church took over intercession, the wording of the prayers should approach the church's language before they disappear. God's mother is named in 27 % of the prayers in Pr2 and 25 % in Pr3, against 12 % in RAK and 5 % in Pr4 – a lead to follow, even though the number of prayers per style group is small.
3. **Other provinces and countries.** Where the church was organised earlier or later, the prayer should have fallen silent earlier or later. A comparison with Denmark needs better records of the crosses on the Danish stones than we have today.
4. **Gifts for the soul.** If intercession moved into the church, gifts for the soul of the dead – to the church or as bridges – may have taken the prayer's place. Bridge building does not clearly increase in our material, and gifts to the church do not show on the stones; other sources are needed here.

## Caveats

- The dating rests on the ornament and is approximate, and the style groups were worked out for the stones of Uppland and Södermanland.
- Prayers are found by searching the normalised text in Rundata. A damaged text can hide a prayer; we therefore tested stones with a preserved end on their own.
- An association in time is not a cause. The hypothesis explains the pattern, but other explanations are possible – for example that a new generation of carvers had other ideals. That the pattern holds with the carver held constant speaks against it being merely a change of generation.
- While working on this we also found an error in how the app leaves out stones that have been moved to churches. It does not affect the main finding, which does not depend on where the stones stand, but the test against the early churches uses the corrected selection. The error has been fixed in the app and is described in the methods.

:::box The essentials in brief
- Around 1035 more than every third dated runestone asked God to help the soul of the dead. Fifty years later almost none did.
- It was not the faith that vanished: the cross remains on a large share of the late stones. It was precisely the prayer that fell silent.
- At the same time the carver's name took the prayer's place at the end of the texts.
- Our hypothesis to test: the prayer left the stones when intercession for the dead became the church's business – the memory stayed on the stone, the care of the soul moved into the church.
:::

## See for yourself

![Christian prayer on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050](/figurer/ac99d4ae73b5032f.webp)
Christian prayer on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050. Source: Vitki's pattern map (r/blogfig.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

![Carver's signature on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050](/figurer/4b3f3c713193e9ea.webp)
Carver's signature on Vitki's pattern map, before and after about 1050. Source: Vitki's pattern map (r/blogfig.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

![The change model's curves: Christian prayer, cross and carver's signature](/figurer/c66cb50dcf72ce3e.webp)
The change model's curves: Christian prayer, cross and carver's signature. Source: Vitki's corpus analysis in R (change.R); Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base (ODbL).

The maps, curves and models come from Vitki, an open tool for runestone research that you can download and run on your own computer from [GitHub](https://github.com/Precatio/runes). The method is described in [METHODS.md](https://github.com/Precatio/runes/blob/main/METHODS.md).
